children: 0454 GMT - The yield curve continues to normalize, plain and simple, Laffer Tengler Investments' Byron Anderson says in a note, adding that "we are firmly set up for higher yields in this environment." "Rate hikes do not solve Iran, oil, AI boom, or inflation," the head of fixed income says. They do increase borrowing costs for everyone else in the market, which will eventually hit labor and the consumer if the Federal Reserve gets aggressive with hikes, he says. Increasing bond issuance, massive debt and deficits, ever-increasing interest costs, and a Fed that's hands-off with guidance and balance-sheet management all point to higher yields. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0442 GMT - The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is being pushed higher by a confluence of factors, according to Madison Investments' Mike Sanders. He lists stronger economic data, heightened Middle East tensions, discussion of a potential diesel export ban and a weak five-year Treasury auction as the drivers. "At this point, it's difficult to point to any single culprit for today's move," the head of fixed income says. The combination of fiscal, economic, geopolitical and supply-side inflation pressures converging has bond markets in less familiar territory, Sanders says. The recent rise in yields can no longer be attributed simply to concerns over the deficit, he adds. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0440 GMT - The difficult question for central banks is how much tightening the market has already done for them, Ken Egan, senior director for sovereigns at KBRA says in a note. "Yields are already high enough to bite into mortgages, corporate borrowing, and investment," he says. Therefore, the market is weighing whether much more policy tightening is actually needed, he says.(emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0432 GMT - Asian bond yields are likely to keep rising and peak only in 1Q to 2Q 2027, as markets continue to price further Fed tightening, ANZ Research's Jennifer Kusuma says in a report. Asian rates are resilient but not immune to the bond-market selloff, she adds. Global bond markets remain under pressure, as rising real yields, elevated energy prices and heavy sovereign issuance push Treasury yields to multiyear highs. ANZ continues to favor safe-haven markets including China and Singapore, while Indonesia and the Philippines remain most exposed to external risks in the near term. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0405 GMT - China's problem isn't the cost of credit--it is the demand for it, say Ajay Rajadhyaksha and Amrut Nashikkar at Barclays Research. Corporate sentiment remains cautious despite a rebound in long-term lending. Corporate borrowing demand is being held back by weak domestic prospects, overcapacity and the continuing property-market downturn, and not because rates are too high, they say in a report. "That distinction matters because it means the PBOC has limited ability to help." Cheaper money doesn't solve a demand problem, they add. (monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0400 GMT - The dollar will likely trade around 4.07 ringgit next week, with U.S. economic data and U.S.-Iran talks in focus, Kenanga economists say in a note. U.S. August PCE core inflation data and September payrolls are likely to be crucial, with stronger-than-expected data potentially raising expectations for the Fed's further rate increases and supporting the dollar, they say. Kenanga expects the dollar to face resistance at 4.090 ringgit, with support at 4.072 ringgit. The dollar is 0.2% lower at 4.0761 ringgit. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0340 GMT - Bank Indonesia could deliver one additional 25 bps rate hike in 4Q, bringing the policy rate to 6.00%, with the timing likely driven by rupiah stability and financial-market conditions, RHB economist Wong Xian Yong says in a note. BI could remain patient in the near term, using forex intervention, liquidity measures and other policy tools to manage temporary currency pressure, he says. The Fed's rate hike could keep pressure on the rupiah, but improved foreign portfolio inflows and higher reserves give BI room to delay a rate move. The November MSCI review remains a key risk to capital flows and the rupiah. A rate hike is therefore likely to be used primarily to support currency and financial stability rather than in response to inflation alone, he adds.(yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0324 GMT - The latest meeting between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping is a "stability summit, not a breakthrough" one, according to Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. "The extension [of a trade truce] lowers the risk of an immediate escalation, but it leaves companies facing much the same uncertainty about the rules they will operate under next year," Chanana says in a research note. Investors are looking for "practical" signals, such as published tariff changes, actual rare-earth shipments, agricultural purchases beyond existing soybean commitments, and any change to chip-export licenses, she says. The outcome looks "too thin to drive a sustained rerating of Chinese equities," she adds. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0320 GMT - The Singapore dollar consolidates against its U.S. counterpart, but prospects of rate increases by the Federal Reserve could weigh on the Asian currency. The U.S. dollar strengthened overnight, as the selloff in global bonds continued, Maybank analysts say in a report. Rising oil prices also add to inflation concerns and reinforce expectations that the Fed's tightening cycle may have further room to run, the analysts add. The U.S. dollar is flat at 1.2791 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0313 GMT - Indonesia's GDP growth could moderate to 5.1% in 2H from 5.45% in 1H, mainly due to slower domestic consumption growth and a larger drag from net exports, RHB economist Wong Xian Yong says in a note. He keeps his 2026 GDP growth estimate at 5.2%, with investment expected to remain the main support as household spending cools. Strong investment in manufacturing, infrastructure and downstream industries should partly offset weaker consumption and external trade. Net exports are expected to keep dragging as imports of capital goods and raw materials outpace subdued exports. Government spending should continue to support domestic demand, although its growth contribution is expected to ease. Wong maintains his 2026 inflation forecast at 2.8%, with upside risks from higher food and energy prices toward year-end and into early 2027.(yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0242 GMT - The Reserve Bank of Australia has concerns about both domestic and global inflation risks, but as it is likely to raise its policy rate next week, it should also be mulling the issue of stronger local GDP growth. Westpac economist Pat Bustamante expects 3Q GDP growth at 2.3% on year, up from 2.1% in 2Q. The economy is proving more resilient than previously feared, he adds. The RBA is unlikely to be comfortable with firmer economic momentum given that it is trying to engineer a period of below-trend growth to ensure inflation returns to its target, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0222 GMT - The Reserve Bank of Australia has more work to do to tame inflation, and by the time it is done, the official cash rate should be at its highest level since 2008, says Adam Boyton, head of Australian economics at ANZ. The RBA will likely raise its policy rate next week and again in November, taking the official cash rate to 4.85%, he adds. The ongoing escalation of the conflict in the Middle East and the tendency of the RBA to view the rise in oil prices as much more of an inflation shock than a growth shock suggest the RBA is prepared to act, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)
